c02.display: Welcome to stop number 3 on our journey, following one little prompt from your keyboard all the way to an answer.
c02.spoken: Welcome to stop number 3 on our journey, following one little prompt from your keyboard all the way to an answer.

c03.display: Here's something strange. The model you chat with has never seen the word "rain". Not once. It only ever sees a number, something like 4,812.
c03.spoken: Here's something strange. The model you chat with has never seen the word "rain". Not once. It only ever sees a number, something like 4,812.

c04.display: Today we find out how your words become numbers, why the model sometimes can't spell, and why this decides how much every message costs.
c04.spoken: Today we find out how your words become numbers, why the model sometimes can't spell, and why this decides how much every message costs.

c05.display: On the route map, we left the Departure Gate, passed through Library Town where the model was trained, and now we're here: Token City, the first stop inside the model itself.

c06.display: Let's start with our traveller, the prompt: "Write a short poem about the rain". On the left of the screen is the prompt as you typed it.
c06.spoken: Let's start with our traveller, the prompt: "Write a short poem about the rain". On the left of the screen is the prompt as you typed it.

c07.display: A computer can't do maths on letters. Underneath, your text is already stored as numbers, one number per character. But a model that works one character at a time would be slow, and a single letter means very little.
c07.spoken: A computer can't do maths on letters. Underneath, your text is already stored as numbers, one number per character. But a model that works one character at a time would be slow, and a single letter means very little.

c08.display: So the model cuts your text into bigger pieces called tokens, and looks each one up in a fixed list, its vocabulary. Every token in that list has an ID number. Those IDs are all the model ever sees.
c08.spoken: So the model cuts your text into bigger pieces called tokens, and looks each one up in a fixed list, its vocabulary. Every token in that list has an ID number. Those Ids are all the model ever sees.

c09.display: So how big should the pieces be? There are three choices, and the word "raindrops" will help us compare them.
c09.spoken: So how big should the pieces be? There are three choices, and the word "raindrops" will help us compare them.

c10.display: Choice one: single characters. R, A, I, N, and so on. The vocabulary is tiny, and nothing is ever unknown. But every sentence becomes a very long sequence, which is slow and expensive.
c10.spoken: Choice one: single characters. R, A, I, N, and so on. The vocabulary is tiny, and nothing is ever unknown. But every sentence becomes a very long sequence, which is slow and expensive.

c11.display: Choice two: whole words. Now "raindrops" is one piece. But there are millions of words, names and typos. Any word missing from the list becomes "unknown", and the model is blind to it.
c11.spoken: Choice two: whole words. Now "raindrops" is one piece. But there are millions of words, names and typos. Any word missing from the list becomes "unknown", and the model is blind to it.

c12.display: Pause and predict. If characters are too small and words are too big, what would you choose?
c12.spoken: Pause and predict. If characters are too small and words are too big, what would you choose?

c13.display: The answer is the middle path: subwords. Common words stay whole. Rare words are built from smaller pieces, like "rain" plus "drops". Every modern chatbot works this way.
c13.spoken: The answer is the middle path: subwords. Common words stay whole. Rare words are built from smaller pieces, like "rain" plus "drops". Every modern chatbot works this way.

c14.display: The most popular way to build that list of subwords is called Byte Pair Encoding, or BPE. The idea fits in one sentence: keep gluing together the pair of pieces that appears most often.
c14.spoken: The most popular way to build that list of subwords is called Byte Pair Encoding, or BPE. The idea fits in one sentence: keep gluing together the pair of pieces that appears most often.

c15.display: Let's run it on a tiny example. Our training text has "rain" 9 times, "rainy" 4 times, "raining" 5 times and "train" 3 times. We start with single letters.
c15.spoken: Let's run it on a tiny example. Our training text has "rain" 9 times, "rainy" 4 times, "raining" 5 times and "train" 3 times. We start with single letters.

c16.display: Now we count every pair of neighbouring letters across all those words. On screen, the bars show the counts.
c16.spoken: Now we count every pair of neighbouring letters across all those words. On screen, the bars show the counts.

c17.display: Pause and predict: which pair wins? Hint: "raining" has it twice.
c17.spoken: Pause and predict: which pair wins? Hint: "raining" has it twice.

c18.display: It's "i" followed by "n", 26 times. So we glue them into one new piece, "in", and add it to the vocabulary.
c18.spoken: It's "i" followed by "n", 26 times. So we glue them into one new piece, "in", and add it to the vocabulary.

c19.display: Then we count again and repeat. "r" plus "a" wins next, 21 times. Then "ra" plus "in" becomes "rain", a whole word as a single token.
c19.spoken: Then we count again and repeat. "r" plus "a" wins next, 21 times. Then "ra" plus "in" becomes "rain", a whole word as a single token.

c20.display: Real tokenizers repeat this tens of thousands of times over huge amounts of text. What's left is a vocabulary where frequent words are one token and rare words are a few.
c20.spoken: Real tokenizers repeat this tens of thousands of times over huge amounts of text. What's left is a vocabulary where frequent words are one token and rare words are a few.

c21.display: Let's look at real tokens. Here's our prompt in a tokenizer. Each coloured block is one token. In most modern tokenizers, every word in it is common enough to be a single token, and the space usually rides along at the start of the word.
c21.spoken: Let's look at real tokens. Here's our prompt in a tokenizer. Each coloured block is one token. In most modern tokenizers, every word in it is common enough to be a single token, and the space usually rides along at the start of the word.

c22.display: Now a rarer word: "tokenization". It's split into "token" and "ization". The model has seen both pieces many times, so it still understands the word.
c22.spoken: Now a rarer word: "tokenization". It's split into "token" and "ization". The model has seen both pieces many times, so it still understands the word.

c23.display: And here's a famous one: "strawberry". One tokenizer splits it into "str", "aw", "berry". Keep that in mind; it comes back in a minute.
c23.spoken: And here's a famous one: "strawberry". One tokenizer splits it into "str", "aw", "berry". Keep that in mind; it comes back in a minute.

c24.display: So why should you care about tokens? Four reasons.
c24.spoken: So why should you care about tokens? Four reasons.

c25.display: One: price. AI services charge per token, for what you send and for what you get back. Long prompts and long answers literally cost more.
c25.spoken: One: price. AI services charge per token, for what you send and for what you get back. Long prompts and long answers literally cost more.

c26.display: Two: memory. A model can only read a limited number of tokens at once, called its context window. Very long chats eventually push old messages out.
c26.spoken: Two: memory. A model can only read a limited number of tokens at once, called its context window. Very long chats eventually push old messages out.

c27.display: Three: languages. Tokenizers are usually trained mostly on English, so the same sentence in Hindi or many other languages can take several times as many tokens, making it slower and costlier.
c27.spoken: Three: languages. Tokenizers are usually trained mostly on English, so the same sentence in Hindi or many other languages can take several times as many tokens, making it slower and costlier.

c28.display: Four: spelling. The model sees "straw" and "berry", not the letters inside them. That's why counting the letters in "strawberry" has tripped up so many chatbots.
c28.spoken: Four: spelling. The model sees "straw" and "berry", not the letters inside them. That's why counting the letters in "strawberry" has tripped up so many chatbots.

c32.display: AI blooper time! In 2023, researchers found a strange token: " SolidGoldMagikarp", a username that had made it into an early GPT vocabulary.

c33.display: When they asked the chatbot of the day to simply repeat it, the model replied with a completely different word. The token was in the vocabulary, but the model had almost never seen it during training, so it had no idea what it meant.
c33.spoken: When they asked the chatbot of the day to simply repeat it, the model replied with a completely different word. The token was in the vocabulary, but the model had almost never seen it during training, so it had no idea what it meant.

c35.display: The myth: one token equals one word.
c35.spoken: The myth: one token equals one word.

c36.display: The reality: in English, a token is about three quarters of a word on average, or roughly four characters. A hundred words is around 130 tokens. Other languages, code and emoji can use many more.
c36.spoken: The reality: in English, a token is about three quarters of a word on average, or roughly four characters. A hundred words is around 130 tokens. Other languages, code and emoji can use many more.

c37.display: And here's your "Use it tomorrow" tip: write shorter prompts to save money on APIs.
c37.spoken: And here's your "Use it tomorrow" tip: write shorter prompts to save money on APIs.

c38.display: Cut polite filler, don't paste a whole document when one section will do, and ask for answers of the length you actually need. Fewer tokens in and out means a lower bill and a faster reply.
c38.spoken: Cut polite filler, don't paste a whole document when one section will do, and ask for answers of the length you actually need. Fewer tokens in and out means a lower bill and a faster reply.

c39.display: Let's stamp the passport. At Token City, your prompt was cut into subword tokens, built by gluing common pairs, and each token became an ID number.
